title: Rare Events, Real Signals: Functional Ensembles as a Computational Substrate in Deep Networks
claim: Interlayer pairwise correlations are weak yet significantly above chance, and the same pattern appears in both artificial networks and biological cortex.
layout: 12 panels in 3 rows by 4 columns, one color per layer pair
description: A 3×4 grid of plots labeled A–L. Each column has its own color: green for L1→L2, blue for L8→L9, orange for L15→L16, and red for mouse V1 L4→L2/3. Row 1 shows overlaid histograms of pairwise STTC values. The observed distribution is colored, the null from circular shifts is grey, and text above each panel gives the mean ± SD. The observed distributions are slightly broader than the null and sit near zero. Row 2 shows histograms of the significant positive edges, with a small inset zooming into the tail. Row 3 shows line plots of the percentage of significant edges against z-score. The colored observed curve stays well above the dashed grey null curve. The mouse column has error bars. The eye goes first to the colored histograms and the coordinated color coding by column.
caption: Inter-Layer Functional Connectivity through Pairwise STTC. Pairwise STTC was computed between the spiking activity of neurons in consecutive layer pairs during inference over the test set of CIFAR100 dataset ("original" data). Columns correspond to layer pairs L2$\rightarrow$L3 (green), L9$\rightarrow$L10 (blue), and L16$\rightarrow$L17 (orange); The final column shows the same analysis in mouse primary visual cortex (V1), computed across cortical layers L4 to L2/3 and aggregated over 5 mice (red). For each panel, a separate null distribution (grey) was computed by randomly circular shifting the spiketrains 150 times. (A–D) Distributions of pairwise STTC values overlaid with null distributions derived from circularly shifted controls. (E–H) Distributions of statistically significant positively correlated edges, defined by a z-score threshold of $z > 4$. (I-L) Percentage of statistically significant edges as a function of z-score. For the mouse data, histograms reflect the distribution of mean values across mice, with error bars denoting SEM; z-scores for all data were computed using the mean and standard deviation of the circular-shift null distributions. The pairwise correlations are weak but statistically significant.
abstract: We investigate how internal representations emerge across hierarchical processing systems by introducing a neuroscience-inspired framework for analyzing deep spiking neural networks (SNN) through the lens of functional connectivity. Drawing on concepts from network neuroscience, we form the first-order functionally connected (1FC) group of a neuron based on its statistically significant pairwise correlations with neurons from the previous layer of a trained SNN architecture. We then track its response properties during inference under various conditions. Our analysis shows that several principles of functional connectivity previously observed in biological visual cortex are preserved in spiking ResNet architectures. These 1FC ensembles display interesting properties: their aggregate cofiring reliably predicts downstream neuronal responses through a robust, ReLU-like input–output relationship, whose gain scales systematically with ensemble size. Reliable encoding of the presented class emerges only during high 1FC cofiring events, which themselves occur infrequently, indicating that informative representations are concentrated in rare but highly coordinated activity patterns. Under uniform random noise, these response profiles are disrupted. This framework enables targeted high-resolution interrogation at specific nodes and pathways. We show that the functional connectivity structure is shaped by learning and this structure breaks under weight permutation. These findings establish 1FC ensembles as a functionally meaningful substrate for input encoding and information transfer.
